video_title: The Real AI Threat Is Two Dudes and a GPU  |  Damien Lewke, CEO & Founder of Nebulock
gist: Nebulock founder Damien Lewke argues the real AI cyber threat is attackers wrapping cheap, guardrail-free open models ("two dudes and a GPU"), not frontier labs. He says Mythos's offensive capabilities flipped the market narrative from 'AI eats cyber' to 'cyber secures AI', driving the re-rating of Palo Alto and CrowdStrike. He also predicts the SIEM will give way to lakehouse architectures and says software supply-chain exposure is the key risk to watch.

themes.theme: Real threat: unguarded open models, not frontier labs

insights.claim: Lewke argues the main AI cyber risk is not frontier labs' agent incidents but attackers building harnesses (tooling) around less-capable, guardrail-free models, such as a DeepSeek-style model (transcribed as 'deep seat') on a single GPU firing at anything with an IP address.
insights.speaker: Damien Lewke (Nebulock CEO)
insights.so_what: Threat volume scales with cheap open-weight models, not frontier-lab capability, so security demand doesn't depend on frontier progress.
insights.quote: The threat is two dudes in a GPU taking pot shots at anybody who's got a publicly exposed interface

insights.claim: Lewke cites Anthropic's threat report from the prior month as flagging attackers who wrap tooling around weaker models to reach competency with no guardrails.
insights.speaker: Damien Lewke (Nebulock CEO)
insights.so_what: Lab threat reports are a leading source for where attacker tradecraft is going.
insights.quote: bad guys building a harness so tooling around much less sophisticated models that gets them to a level of competency with no guardrails

insights.claim: Lewke says frontier-lab incidents like the OpenAI/Hugging Face episode come from reward-seeking systems doing what they are measured against, and focusing on them misses the bigger risk.
insights.speaker: Damien Lewke (Nebulock CEO)
insights.so_what: Headline lab incidents may be a distraction from mass, low-sophistication AI attacks.
insights.quote: a system that is designed to get to a reward as quickly as possible is going to do what you measure it against

insights.claim: Breach reporting is a lagging indicator: disclosed incidents are months old, and six months is a lifetime in AI, so more AI-driven breaches are already in the pipeline.
insights.speaker: Damien Lewke (Nebulock CEO)
insights.so_what: Expect a continuing stream of breach disclosures that keeps security top of mind and budgets up.
insights.quote: Breach reporting is a lagging indicator.

insights.claim: Lewke says that as soon as ChatGPT launched he expected LLMs to be used quickly to reverse-engineer binaries and build offensive tools, and that defense is structurally harder because breaking things is easier than rebuilding them.
insights.speaker: Damien Lewke (Nebulock CEO)
insights.so_what: AI favors offense over defense in cyber, which gives a structural tailwind to defensive spending.
insights.quote: it's so much easier to figure out how to break down something in security than it is to build it back up

insights.claim: Lewke says enterprises now have to secure AI internally and defend against AI externally at once, while also struggling to see shadow AI, such as a developer running an open-weights model or Open Claw with data access despite an approved Claude Enterprise.
insights.speaker: Damien Lewke (Nebulock CEO)
insights.so_what: Visibility and identity tools for both humans and agents are an urgent area of spend.
insights.quote: there's nothing stopping Damian the developer from downloading and running Open Claw or an open-source open-weights model that has access to data

insights.claim: Lewke says the earlier selloff in cyber stocks (the 'SaaS-pocalypse') came from investors confusing AI code-scanning tools like OpenAI's Aardvark and Claude Code Security with endpoint security, which they don't replace.
insights.speaker: Damien Lewke (Nebulock CEO)
insights.so_what: Selloffs driven by AI-displacement fears can misread which product categories are actually at risk.
insights.quote: code scanning and code security is not endpoint security

insights.claim: Lewke says the turn in cyber stocks came around late March/early April with Mythos and its announced advanced offensive cyber capabilities, later echoed by open-weights models like GLM-53 claiming Mythos-level ability, which shifted the story from 'AI eats cyber' to 'cyber secures against AI.'
insights.speaker: Damien Lewke (Nebulock CEO)
insights.so_what: Each advance in offensive AI capability supports security valuations.
insights.quote: Instead of AI eating cyber, uh we need cyber to secure against AI and secure AI.

insights.claim: Lewke's valuation framework is that as AI offensive capability grows over time, the value of security investments grows with it, so today's prices are a bet on that path.
insights.speaker: Damien Lewke (Nebulock CEO)
insights.so_what: Cyber multiples are tied to how fast offensive AI advances; if that progress stalls, the thesis weakens.
insights.quote: And what you're really seeing is a bet on the future.

insights.claim: Lewke says security has become a strategic budget priority to a degree he can't recall in his career, citing Mythos, the summer OpenAI/Hugging Face incident and a recent run of breach disclosures.
insights.speaker: Damien Lewke (Nebulock CEO)
insights.so_what: Points to strong security budget growth on the demand side.
insights.quote: We are seeing security become a strategic priority for businesses in a way that I personally cannot recall ever in my history

insights.claim: Nathan notes that Palo Alto went from about $150 in March to about $450 (about 10% off recent highs), at roughly a $270B market cap; together with CrowdStrike that is about $500B of market cap on about $20B of expected revenue this year.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Cyber leaders are priced at extreme multiples of revenue.

insights.claim: Nathan says Palo Alto may do about $14B in sales this year and $16.5B next, trading at about 81x earnings and 20x sales, which makes it one of the most expensive stocks in the market for modest growth and leaves it vulnerable to any demand or capex pullback.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Rich multiples leave little room for error if spending slows.
insights.quote: It trades about 81 times earnings this year, 20 times sales.

insights.claim: Lewke argues that a slowdown in enterprise AI adoption or data center buildout would cause at most a slight tail-off in cyber demand, because securing AI is a small slice of incumbents' revenue and attackers using AI is the real driver.
insights.speaker: Damien Lewke (Nebulock CEO)
insights.so_what: Cyber spend may be less tied to the AI capex cycle than the market assumes.
insights.quote: securing AI, which is directly related to enterprise AI adoption, is like a small small sliver of the revenue that Palo Alto and CrowdStrike and a lot of folks make

themes.theme: Software supply chain as the key exposure

insights.claim: Asked which public companies are most exposed, Lewke (saying it is not investment advice) points to organizations with software supply-chain dependencies as the most likely to be hit by AI-based attacks.
insights.speaker: Damien Lewke (Nebulock CEO)
insights.so_what: Screen holdings for upstream software dependencies, since that is where AI-scaled attacks spread.
insights.quote: If I were an investor, I'd I'd be really heavily scrutinizing organizations with the software supply chain dependency.

insights.claim: Lewke cites the recent ConnectWise breach (a compromised upstream Microsoft service) and the Salesloft breach about 18 months earlier as examples of supply-chain compromises spreading downstream.
insights.speaker: Damien Lewke (Nebulock CEO)
insights.so_what: Upstream SaaS and IT-management vendors are concentrated points of contagion risk.

insights.claim: Lewke says AI does not dramatically raise the risk to critical infrastructure (grid, water, power), since those networks are largely segmented and often need physical or near-perimeter access; the threat already exists, as Colonial Pipeline and Volt Typhoon show.
insights.speaker: Damien Lewke (Nebulock CEO)
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the 'p(catastrophe)' framing: AI adds some risk, but not a step change.
insights.quote: I don't think AI makes it dramatically easier to target those systems. It does make it easier though

themes.theme: Market structure: SIEM convergence and AI-native challengers

insights.claim: Lewke says four security markets are converging into one: SIEM (Splunk, Elastic), MDR/MSSPs, AI SOCs, and insider threat/UEBA analytics.
insights.speaker: Damien Lewke (Nebulock CEO)
insights.so_what: Expect consolidation; vendors stuck in a single category face pressure.

insights.claim: Lewke predicts the SIEM as we know it will go away as customers move to data lake and lakehouse architectures, with an orchestration 'security brain' sitting on top.
insights.speaker: Damien Lewke (Nebulock CEO)
insights.so_what: Bearish for legacy SIEM data-store economics; bullish for lakehouse and orchestration layers.
insights.quote: I actually think that the SIM as we understand it will go away.

insights.claim: Nebulock directly replaces insider-risk/UEBA analytics platforms, sometimes replaces MDR providers and AI SOCs, but does not yet displace Splunk.
insights.speaker: Damien Lewke (Nebulock CEO)
insights.so_what: Shows where AI-native challengers are taking budget first.

insights.claim: Lewke says Nebulock's pitch is being source-agnostic, so enterprises re-evaluating their security spend can avoid locking into one ecosystem and the churn of migrating off a platform; it partners with large players like CrowdStrike and Palo Alto.
insights.speaker: Damien Lewke (Nebulock CEO)
insights.so_what: Platform lock-in by incumbents creates an opening for vendor-neutral layers.

insights.claim: Nebulock says it has run more than 375 million threat hunts and surfaced more than 12,000 incidents over two years, building a proprietary behavioral detection dataset.
insights.speaker: Damien Lewke (Nebulock CEO)
insights.so_what: Proprietary detection data is the moat AI-native security vendors claim.
insights.quote: We've run over 375 million threat hunts in the past 2 years. We've surfaced over 12,000 incidents

insights.claim: Lewke reports strong traction with high-growth early-stage companies and says 50-person startups now hire full-time security staff, which was never a conversation before, because AI-native, software-dependent firms are being targeted (e.g., the Vercel breach).
insights.speaker: Damien Lewke (Nebulock CEO)
insights.so_what: Security spending is starting much earlier in a company's life, widening the addressable market.
insights.quote: they're hiring full-time resources as like a 50-person company. That was never a conversation.

themes.theme: AI adoption reality and agents as insiders

insights.claim: Lewke says enterprise AI adoption is slower than headlines suggest: about 5% of enterprises had adopted AI at the end of last year versus about 30% now.
insights.speaker: Damien Lewke (Nebulock CEO)
insights.so_what: AI adoption, and the security spend tied to it, still has a long runway.
insights.quote: I think at the end of last year it was 5% of enterprises have adopted AI, and right about now it's at about 30%.

insights.claim: Lewke argues AI agents should be treated as insiders: competent but risky non-deterministic systems that need visibility, hygiene and enforcement controls. He cites Camille Stewart Gloster (now at CrowdStrike).
insights.speaker: Damien Lewke (Nebulock CEO)
insights.so_what: Identity and insider-threat tooling extends naturally to agent governance.
insights.quote: you got to treat an agent as an insider

insights.claim: At MIT, an AI-for-engineering-design class grew from 13 students in fall 2022 to 133 in spring 2023 after ChatGPT launched.
insights.speaker: Damien Lewke (Nebulock CEO)
insights.so_what: A concrete measure of how quickly talent moved toward AI.
